prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect

statement.case_for: B044 remains my first choice after reading the colleagues' openings. It is a discovery tied to a nameable phenomenon in nature: protected helical edge channels in a two-dimensional insulator, predicted through the Z2 classification of Kane and Mele and then observed in HgTe quantum wells in Molenkamp's laboratory. The idea reorganised band theory, produced the three-dimensional topological insulators and a large materials programme, and has been confirmed by independent groups over roughly two decades with a stable interpretation. It has the strongest opening support on the shortlist (two first places, four top-three placements, six of eight members ranking it), and that support is mirrored by substantive agreement in the written assessments of Eriksson, Lindroth, Olsson, Johansson and Kroll. A theory-plus-experiment prize of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the cleanest allocation available within the credited names, and it fits the principle of rewarding the discovery first and then identifying the people behind it.
statement.case_against: The credit is not clean. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe/CdTe as the concrete material that Molenkamp's group then measured, and Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, Roy, Hsieh and Hasan carried the idea to three dimensions, none of whom (apart from Kane and Mele) are in the credited set. Awarding Molenkamp without the proposal that told him where to look could be read as unbalanced, and the topological theme was already recognised in 2016 for Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz, so some members may see this as a second prize on the same conceptual ground. I take the latter objection less seriously, because the 2016 prize concerned topological phase transitions and quantum Hall-type phases, whereas time-reversal-invariant topological insulators are a distinct, symmetry-protected class. The attribution problem is real and I cannot resolve it from the supplied names alone.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock (B024) first as the clearest case of better measurement opening new physics, and places B044 fifth, outside his specialism and partly absorbed after the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I agree that B024 is a clean, two-name, mature case with an unambiguous inventor in Katori and a decisive realiser in Ye, and I keep it as an alternative. But I disagree that B044 is partly absorbed by 2016. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall-type topology; Z2 insulators protected by time-reversal symmetry with no magnetic field are a different class, and the field of topological materials that followed is arguably larger than what 2016 recognised. The clock case is strong on precision, but B044 reveals a new phase of matter, and I place that above a metrological improvement that builds on already recognised ion-clock and comb foundations.

responses.point: Eriksson puts dynamical mean-field theory (B037) first for its decades of use and the DFT+DMFT link to real materials, with B044 second and the 2016 prize leaving this strand unrecognised.
responses.response: I share Eriksson's view that B044 is mature and that the 2016 prize did not cover it, and I respect the lasting impact of DMFT. My reservation about B037 is its framing: it is a method and framework rather than a discovery about nature, which Eriksson himself flags, and the credit is awkward with Metzner and Mueller-Hartmann outside the three names. B044 gives a sharper discovery statement with a measurable signature. I would not rule out B037 for a later year, but I do not think it should displace B044 now.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, ranks the IceCube diffuse neutrino flux (B019) first, valuing a new detector concept and a new window on the universe, and proposes Halzen as sole laureate.
responses.response: I find the astronomy compelling and I ranked B019 fourth. My difficulty is attribution: a sole prize to Halzen for a large-collaboration instrument is hard to defend, and the credited names support nothing wider, so the committee would be choosing between an incomplete configuration and one it cannot name. The B044 trio is complete as supplied. If Pearce can argue that Halzen alone captures the discovery, I would want to hear how the committee addresses the other builders of AMANDA and IceCube.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first, places B044 third as plainly past due, and ranks B020 fourth as somewhat early because the superconducting mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I agree with her maturity assessment of B044 and with her caution that the BHZ and 3D-topological-insulator allocation remains unresolved. On B020 I am a little more generous than she is: the existence of correlated insulators and superconductivity in magic-angle graphene is firmly established even if the pairing mechanism is not, and I ranked it third. But I accept that a mechanism still in flux makes it the weaker of the two condensed matter candidates this year, which is why I keep it as an alternative and not as a partner.

uncertainties: How the committee should treat Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the three-dimensional topological insulator contributors, given that they are outside the credited names; I have not independently checked the priority chronology of Kane-Mele and BHZ.
Whether colleagues who rank B044 lower treat the 2016 prize as covering the topic; I think it does not, but this is a judgement about overlap, not a settled fact.

Whether a prize with one theory part and one experiment part should be structured as two parts; the credited names restrict the total to three people, so a single part with three names is the workable form.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented connections (PhD supervisor David Gross, early mentor Hector Rubinstein, co-author Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not appear among the credited names. My own field is high-energy theory and cosmology, not condensed matter, which limits my independent assessment of the topological insulator literature.
